subject: Geografi
title: Sustainable development and climate change
sourceSummary: What sustainable development means in terms of ecological, social and economic sustainability, how the greenhouse effect and climate change are connected, their global consequences, and the basic idea behind the UN's Global Goals.
topics: the greenhouse effect and climate change

questions.prompt: Which three dimensions is sustainable development usually divided into?
questions.opener: Think of sustainability as three puzzle pieces that all need to be in place at once for development to last.
choices: Ecological, social and economic sustainability
Political, religious and cultural sustainability
Local, national and global sustainability
Historical, present-day and future sustainability
questions.explanation: Sustainable development is usually divided into ecological sustainability (not harming nature and ecosystems), social sustainability (people having good living conditions, justice and security) and economic sustainability (the economy developing without using up resources that future generations will need). All three are needed at the same time for development to be sustainable in the long run.

questions.prompt: A company builds a factory that creates many jobs and strengthens the economy, but it releases large amounts of toxins into a nearby lake that the local population fishes in. Which type of sustainability is failing here?
questions.opener: Think about which of the three dimensions is directly harmed by the pollution.
choices: Economic sustainability
Ecological sustainability (and thereby also social sustainability, since people's health and livelihoods are affected)
No sustainability dimension is affected
Only political sustainability
questions.explanation: The pollution damages the lake's ecosystem (ecological sustainability) and at the same time affects the people who depend on fishing for food and income (social sustainability). This shows that the three dimensions are connected — you cannot just look at the economic profit but must also weigh in the effects on the environment and on people.

questions.topic: the greenhouse effect and climate change
questions.prompt: What is the natural greenhouse effect, and why is it fundamentally necessary for life on Earth?
questions.opener: Without any greenhouse effect at all, the Earth would be much colder than it is today.
choices: It is a modern phenomenon caused solely by humans, and entirely harmful
Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trap heat from the sun and keep the Earth warm enough for life
It describes how growing plants in greenhouses works
It is about the ozone layer breaking down
questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect occurs when gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour in the atmosphere trap some of the sun's heat instead of letting it radiate out into space. Without this natural effect, the Earth's average temperature would be far below freezing. The problem today is that human emissions AMPLIFY the effect beyond what is natural.

questions.topic: the greenhouse effect and climate change
questions.prompt: Which human activity contributes MOST to the enhanced greenhouse effect globally?
questions.opener: Think about what releases large amounts of carbon dioxide that would otherwise have stayed locked in the ground.
choices: Burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas
People breathing
It raining more in some places
The Earth rotating on its own axis
questions.explanation: Burning fossil fuels in industry, transport and electricity production releases large amounts of carbon dioxide that has been locked in the ground for millions of years, making it the single largest source of human greenhouse gas emissions. Deforestation also contributes significantly, since trees would otherwise capture carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a direct consequence of the Earth's average temperature rising?
questions.opener: Think about what happens to ice and glaciers when it gets warmer.
choices: Sea levels rise because glaciers and ice sheets melt and because seawater expands as it warms
The Earth's orbit around the sun changes
The number of continents increases
The ozone layer repairs itself automatically
questions.explanation: As the average temperature rises, glaciers and ice sheets melt (for example in Greenland and Antarctica), and seawater also expands as it warms. Both effects cause sea levels to rise, which threatens low-lying coastal areas and island nations with flooding.

questions.prompt: Why are low-income countries often hit hardest by the consequences of climate change, even though they have historically emitted the least greenhouse gases?
questions.opener: Think about the difference between being EXPOSED to a risk and having the RESOURCES to protect yourself against it.
choices: They are always located closer to the equator and nothing else matters
They often have fewer economic resources to protect themselves against, for example, drought, flooding and crop failure
Climate change only affects rich countries
Low-income countries cause the most emissions today
questions.explanation: Many low-income countries are heavily dependent on agriculture and have fewer economic resources to build protection against extreme weather, irrigation systems or disaster preparedness, which makes them especially vulnerable to drought, flooding and crop failure. This is a key injustice in the climate issue: the countries that have contributed least to emissions are often hit hardest by the consequences.

questions.prompt: Explain the idea behind the UN's Global Goals (Agenda 2030) and why the Global Goals are considered to be interconnected.
questions.opener: Think about why you cannot solve, for example, poverty or the climate issue entirely separately from one another.
questions.answer: The UN's Global Goals, also known as Agenda 2030, are 17 goals that the world's countries have agreed on in order to achieve sustainable development by 2030 — they cover everything from eradicating poverty and hunger to gender equality, clean water, climate action and peaceful societies. The goals are considered to be interconnected because progress in one area often affects others: for example, climate change (goal 13) can worsen poverty (goal 1) and hunger (goal 2) through crop failure, while better education (goal 4) often leads to both reduced poverty and greater gender equality (goal 5). Sustainability challenges therefore cannot be solved one by one in isolation — the whole picture must be considered.
steps: Agenda 2030 contains 17 Global Goals that the UN's member states have agreed on.
The goals cover ecological, social and economic sustainability together (e.g. climate, poverty, gender equality, education).
The goals are interlinked: a change in one goal often affects several others, positively or negatively.
Example: climate change (goal 13) can worsen hunger (goal 2) through crop failure, which in turn increases poverty (goal 1).
Conclusion: sustainable development requires working on the goals together, not separately.

questions.prompt: Summarise sustainable development and climate change: concepts, causes and consequences.
questions.opener: Gather the key concepts into a compact overview for quick revision.
questions.answer: Sustainable development: development that meets today's needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs · three dimensions: ecological (environment and ecosystems), social (justice, health, security) and economic (resources lasting in the long run) sustainability. The greenhouse effect: a natural process in which greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane and others) trap heat in the atmosphere · human emissions from fossil fuels and deforestation AMPLIFY the effect. Consequences: rising average temperature · melting glaciers and ice → rising sea levels · more extreme weather (drought, flooding, storms) · crop failure and threats to food supply · low-income countries often hit hardest despite having the lowest emissions. The UN's Global Goals (Agenda 2030): 17 goals for sustainable development by 2030 · the goals are interconnected and must be tackled together.

questions.prompt: What definition is usually used for sustainable development (from the 1987 Brundtland Report)?
questions.opener: Think about the balance between meeting needs NOW and not destroying the opportunities of those who come AFTER.
choices: Development that meets today's needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Development that focuses solely on economic growth
Development that stops all change in society
Development that only applies to rich countries
questions.explanation: This definition, from the UN's 1987 Brundtland Report, is the most widely used definition of sustainable development and emphasises the balance between the needs of present and future generations.

questions.topic: the greenhouse effect and climate change
questions.prompt: Which greenhouse gas is the most common and most discussed in connection with human emissions?
questions.opener: This gas is formed, among other things, by burning fossil fuels.
choices: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Noble gases
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the most discussed greenhouse gas because human burning of fossil fuels releases very large amounts of it. Methane and nitrous oxide are other important greenhouse gases, but in smaller total volumes.

questions.topic: the greenhouse effect and climate change
questions.prompt: What is the phenomenon called, beyond burning fossil fuels, where removing large forest areas reduces the Earth's ability to absorb carbon dioxide?
questions.opener: The word is the opposite of planting forest.
choices: Deforestation
Urbanisation
Erosion
Colonisation
questions.explanation: Deforestation means forest is cut down or burned, which both releases carbon dioxide that was stored in the trees and reduces the Earth's overall ability to absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: What is a likely consequence of more frequent and intense heatwaves due to climate change?
questions.opener: Think about what extreme heat does to both crops and human health.
choices: Increased risk of crop failure, heat-related health problems and wildfires
No effect at all on agriculture or health
Automatically cooler climate globally
Reduced risk of drought
questions.explanation: More frequent and intense heatwaves increase the risk of crop failure through drying out, heat-related illness and death, and favour the outbreak of wildfires - several connected consequences of the same underlying cause.

questions.prompt: By which year are the UN's Global Goals (Agenda 2030) meant to be achieved at the latest?
questions.opener: The name of the agenda reveals the year.
questions.explanation: Agenda 2030 was adopted by UN member states in 2015, with the goal that the 17 Global Goals be achieved by 2030 at the latest.

questions.prompt: A municipality is planning to build a new housing development on previously undeveloped forest land near the town. Explain how the decision can be analysed using the three sustainability dimensions.
questions.opener: Go through ecological, social and economic sustainability one at a time, then weigh them against each other.
questions.answer: Ecological sustainability is affected because forest and its ecosystem disappear. Social sustainability could be strengthened if more people gain access to housing, but could also be weakened if nearby residents lose recreational space. Economic sustainability could benefit from increased tax revenue and housing construction - the municipality needs to weigh all three dimensions against each other rather than focusing on just one.
steps: Ecological sustainability: the forest land is a habitat for plants and animals, and developing it can harm the local ecosystem and reduce the municipality's green spaces.
Social sustainability: more housing can solve a housing shortage and give more people a secure home, but neighbours may simultaneously lose access to nature-based recreation.
Economic sustainability: new housing can give the municipality increased tax revenue and strengthen the local economy through construction and new residents.
A sustainable solution tries to balance all three dimensions, for example by preserving part of the forest as green space while still building housing.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of ECONOMIC sustainability?
questions.opener: Think about which of the three dimensions specifically concerns resources and the economy over time.
choices: That a business can keep generating income and jobs without using up resources that will be needed in the future
Protecting endangered species
Everyone having access to clean water
Reducing carbon dioxide emissions
questions.explanation: Economic sustainability is about economic activity being able to continue in the long run without using up resources that future generations will need. Protecting species and reducing emissions instead belong to ecological sustainability, and clean water for all is an example of social sustainability.
